paragraphs.heading: The hidden body of a fungus
paragraphs.text: Mycelium is the root-like body of a fungus. It is a mass of hyphae, slender threads that branch, tangle and join up with one another. Fungal colonies made of mycelium live in and on soil and many other surfaces. A colony can be too small to see, or it can spread across thousands of acres, as in Armillaria.

paragraphs.heading: How a fungus eats
paragraphs.text: A fungus takes in its food through its mycelium, in two steps. First, the hyphae release enzymes onto or into the food source. These enzymes break large biological molecules into smaller units such as monomers. The mycelium then absorbs those units by processes called facilitated diffusion and active transport.

paragraphs.heading: Two mycelia make one
paragraphs.text: A single spore typically sprouts into what is called a monokaryotic mycelium, and this kind cannot reproduce sexually. If two compatible mycelia of that kind meet and join, the result is a dikaryotic mycelium. That joined mycelium may then produce fruiting bodies such as mushrooms.

paragraphs.heading: Its place in nature
paragraphs.text: Mycelia matter on land and in water because they break down plant material. They add to the organic part of soil, and as they grow they return carbon dioxide to the air. The mycelium of mycorrhizal fungi helps most plants take up water and nutrients more efficiently and gives them resistance to some plant diseases. Mycelium is also an important food for many soil invertebrates, and mycelial networks can carry water and spikes of electrical potential.

paragraphs.heading: Cleaning up and composting
paragraphs.text: Petroleum products and some pesticides are built on carbon, so fungi could use them as a carbon source and may clear them from soil, unless the chemicals poison the fungus. This kind of cleanup is called mycoremediation. Mats of mycelium have also been proposed as living filters that remove chemicals and microbes from soil and water, an idea called mycofiltration. In compost, fungi break down materials such as lignin that many other composting microbes cannot. Turning a backyard compost heap often uncovers networks of mycelium on the rotting matter.

paragraphs.heading: Growing new materials
paragraphs.text: Mycelium grown on farm waste can stand in for polystyrene and plastic packaging. It has also been made into furniture and artificial leather, one of its main commercial uses. For leather, mycelium is grown on forestry products such as sawdust, in air rich in carbon dioxide with controlled humidity and temperature. The mat that forms on top is dried, treated with chemicals, pressed to the right thickness and stamped with a pattern.

paragraphs.heading: Building with mycelium
paragraphs.text: Mycelium appeals to builders because it is light, biodegradable and can be grown from waste. It is fairly strong for its weight and has much lower embodied energy than traditional building materials. Research suggests it does not give off toxic resins in a fire, because it chars much like mass timber. It also absorbs 70–75% of sound at frequencies of 1500 Hz or less. One drawback is that, on its own, it resists squeezing poorly, with a compressive strength of only 0.1–0.2 MPa.
